_readme: Working English translation of Theon's Progymnasmata, made for this app directly from
the public-domain Greek of Walz (Rhetores Graeci) that build-theon.py ingests. It is an
original translation: Kennedy's SBL 2003 English is under copyright and was not used.
Keys are 'chapter.paragraph', matching the numbering build-theon.py emits.
build-theon.py merges these into the `text` field of each paragraph, and only marks the
work as no-longer-Greek-only once EVERY paragraph has an English rendering — so a
partly-translated work never ships blank English columns to students.
Hand-polish freely; square brackets mark words supplied for sense, and (†) marks a spot
1.1: The orators of old, and above all those who won distinction, held that a man ought not to take up rhetoric in any fashion before he had somehow laid hold of philosophy and been filled with the largeness of mind that comes from it. But nowadays most are so far from any grasp of such studies that they rush off to public speaking without taking the least share in what are called the general subjects; and — crudest of all — without even having been trained in the exercises that properly belong to it, they launch into forensic and deliberative cases, learning the potter's trade, as the proverb has it, on a wine-jar. Now as for the other things a man who intends to practise oratory must learn, let others write of them; but what it is necessary to know, and to be reasonably well trained in, before taking up a case — these I shall now try to hand on. Not that others have not written on these matters as well; but I hope that I too may contribute something not small to those who set out to speak. For we have not only devised some further exercises in addition to those already handed down, but have also tried to give a definition of each, so that a student asked what each of them is may be able to say — for instance, that a fable is a fictitious account picturing a truth. We have further shown their differences from one another, handed on the starting points for the compositions belonging to each, and shown besides how one might use them to best advantage.
1.2:
That they are thoroughly useful to those taking up the power of rhetoric is likewise no secret. For the man who has delivered a narrative and a fable well and in many ways will also compose history well, and that which in cases is specially called the individual narrative — for history is nothing other than a system of narrative. And when a man is able to refute or confirm these, he falls little short of those who plead cases; for everything we do in forensic cases is present here too. First there is an introduction and a narrative; then we try to meet each of the things said in the narrative or the fable, and to furnish a refutation of each; and further we take thought how we shall arrange each of the arguments well, and we amplify and we disparage, and all the rest, about which it would take long to speak at present.

Moreover, the exercise through the chreia produces not only a certain power of words, but also a sound character, since we are training ourselves in the sayings of the wise. The so-called commonplace and ecphrasis have an evident benefit, since among the ancients all the historians everywhere used ecphrasis to the fullest, and the orators the commonplace. Impersonation, too, is not only a historical exercise but a rhetorical, dialogical, and poetic one, and is most useful in daily life and in our conversations with one another, and most serviceable for coming to grips with books. It is for this reason that we praise Homer first of all, because he has assigned to each of the persons he brings on the words that suit him; and that we find fault with Euripides, because his Hecuba philosophizes out of season.

And indeed the exercise of comparison is useful in forensic speeches as well, when we compare wrongs with wrongs or benefits with benefits; and likewise in encomia, when we set achievements side by side; while in deliberative speeches the benefit is altogether plain, for the words of those who give counsel are concerned with what is preferable. As for the thesis, what need one say? For it differs from the case in nothing except that it leaves persons, place, time, manner, and cause undefined. A thesis, for instance, is whether men under siege should send an army abroad; a case, whether the Athenians, under siege by the Peloponnesians, should send an army to Sicily. Likewise the accusation and defence of laws is not the smallest part of a case: the finest of Demosthenes' speeches, at any rate, are those in which some law or decree is in dispute — I mean the speech On the Crown, and those against Androtion and Timocrates, and against Leptines, and against Aristocrates; for it made little difference that Aristocrates proposed not a law but a decree.

As for the encomium, I am not myself unaware that it is a species of case — for there are three species of case: the encomiastic, which Aristotle's school called epideictic; the forensic; and the deliberative. But since we are often accustomed to set the younger students to write encomia, I have on that account placed it among the preliminary exercises; and at the same time I have deferred the precise technical treatment of it to its proper place, and have made the instruction here simpler.

Reading, as one of the older men said — Apollonius of Rhodes, I think — is the nourishment of style; for having our souls stamped from noble models, we shall imitate them most nobly. And who would not gladly welcome listening, taking over readily what others have worked out with toil? But just as it is of no use to those who wish to paint to study the works of Apelles and Protogenes and Antiphilus unless they also set their own hands to painting, so for those who intend to practise oratory neither the speeches of their elders, nor abundance of ideas, nor purity of diction, nor well-fitted composition, nor elegant listening, nor in short any of the fine things in rhetoric is of use, unless each man also trains himself by writing every day.

Paraphrase is not useless, as some have said or supposed. For they say that speaking well comes about once and cannot be done twice; but these men have gone quite astray from the truth. For the mind is not moved by a single thing in only one way, so as to bring out the impression that has fallen upon it in one and the same manner, but in several ways: now as we make a statement, now as we ask a question, now as we inquire, now as we pray, now as we bring out the thought in some other manner. Nothing therefore prevents what we have imagined from being brought out equally well in all these ways. There are witnesses to this among the poets and the historians; and in short all the ancients are seen to have used paraphrase to excellent effect, reshaping not only their own work but also one another's.

Archilochus, for instance, recasts Homer. Homer says that such is the mind of men upon the earth as the father of men and gods brings on the day; and Archilochus, that such is the spirit that comes to mortal men, Glaucus son of Leptines, as Zeus brings on the day. Again, Homer described the capture of a city in this fashion: the men they kill, and fire lays the city waste, and others lead away the children and the deep-girdled women. Demosthenes did so thus: when we were travelling to Delphi, we could not but see all this — houses razed, walls stripped away, a countryside empty of men in their prime, a few poor women and little children, and pitiable old men. And Aeschines thus: look with your minds upon their disasters, and think you see the city being taken — walls thrown down, houses burning, temples plundered, women and children led away into slavery, old men and old women learning too late to give up their freedom.

Again, Thucydides says that there is envy toward the living where there is rivalry, but that what is out of the way is honoured with a goodwill that meets no opposition. Theopompus says that he knows that many scrutinize the living with ill will, but that toward the dead the passage of years relaxes men's envy. And Demosthenes thus: who among all men does not know that toward all the living there attaches some envy, greater or less, but that no one, not even an enemy, hates the dead?

And indeed Philistus transferred the whole Attic war in his Sicilian history from Thucydides; and Demosthenes, in the speech against Meidias, took over into it the work of Lysias and Lycurgus from their speeches on outrage, and that of Isaeus from the speech against Diocles for outrage. You would find, too, in Isocrates' Panegyricus the material of Lysias' Funeral Oration and of his Olympiacus. And indeed Demosthenes often paraphrases himself, not only transferring elsewhere what he had said in other speeches, but even within a single speech he is plainly found to have said the same things countless times, escaping his hearers' notice by the variety of his expression.

In the speech against Meidias he says: who of us does not know that the cause of many such things happening is that wrongdoers go unpunished, and that the one cause of no one committing outrage hereafter is that each man caught should pay the penalty that is fitting? And in the speech against Aristocrates — and the same in the speech against Androtion: if something has ever been done contrary to the laws and you have imitated it, you would not on that account be justly acquitted, but on the contrary should be convicted all the more because of it; for just as, had one of those men been convicted, you would not have proposed this, so if you pay the penalty, another will not propose it.

In the Philippics he goes on saying the same things up and down; and in the speech against Leptines he has said not seldom that one must not take away from benefactors what has been given them; and in the speech On the Crown the point that it was not just to accuse him on the outcome of what had been done, but to test each measure of policy as it came, is scattered through the whole speech; and as for the ransoming of the prisoners, who does not know how it is harped upon in the speech On the False Embassy?

And indeed the species called elaboration is useful in many other places, but especially in second speeches; and refutation in written replies.
1.3: We shall arrange the exercises themselves thus. First we begin from the chreia, for it is short and easy to remember; then the fable and the narrative, apart from their refutation and confirmation, for these seem in a way to come after the rest. For it is agreed by all that the orator's task is both to prove what is in dispute and to amplify what has been proved. Now the demonstrative speech comes first in nature and in use, and the amplificatory follows; for one must first convict a man as a traitor, and then rouse the hearers against treason as a great crime. Yet it does not follow that, because we said proof comes before amplification in nature, it stands so with training as well; quite the contrary, for the easiest come before the harder, and it is easier to amplify what is evident than to prove what is not. Therefore, when we ourselves begin to argue out of our own resources and to refute or confirm, we shall begin from the commonplace, then ecphrasis, then impersonation; then we shall train in encomia, then in comparisons — for these are agreed upon and admit of no dispute. After these we shall make our practice on the disputed exercises as well. First of them is the refutation of chreiai, then of Aesop's tales and of historical and mythical narratives, then of theses, and next of laws. Reading and listening and paraphrase we shall use from the very beginning; but elaboration, and much more refutation, only when we have acquired some facility.
2.1:
First of all, the teacher of each exercise must collect good examples from the ancient writings and set the young to learn them by heart. Of the chreia, for instance, there is the one in Plato in the first book of the Republic: someone once came up to Sophocles the poet and said, How are you, Sophocles, in regard to the pleasures of love? Are you still able to consort with women? And he said, Hush, man; I have most gladly escaped from them, as though I had run away from a raging and savage master.

Of the fable, there is the flute-player in Herodotus, and the horse in Philistus, and the examples in each of them in the first and second books; and in the twentieth book of Theopompus' Philippics the fable of war and insolence, which Philip relates to the chief magistrates of the Chalcidians; and in the second book of Xenophon's Memorabilia the fable of the dog and the sheep.

The finest examples of narrative would be, among the mythical, Plato's in the second book of the Republic about the ring of Gyges, and in the Symposium about the birth of Love, and about the things in Hades in the Phaedo and the tenth book of the Republic; and in Theopompus, in the eighth book of the Philippics, the story of Silenus. Among the factual, there is the account of Cylon in Herodotus and Thucydides, and of Amphilochus son of Amphiaraus in the third book of Thucydides, and the story of Cleobis and Biton from the first book of Herodotus; and Ephorus in his seventh book and Philistus in his first have the story of the coming of Daedalus to Cocalus, king of the Sicanians. You will find, too, in Demosthenes' speech On the False Embassy a spare and polished narrative about the Olympic games celebrated by Philip after the capture of Olynthus.

We have refutations and confirmations among the ancients as well — of chreiai and maxims and pronouncements and the like. To this species would belong what is said by Ephorus in the eleventh book of his Histories against the pronouncements laid down by the older writers concerning the Nile. Of mythical narratives there is the passage in the second book of Herodotus about those things which the Greeks tell as tales — how the Egyptians tried to sacrifice Heracles to Zeus when he visited them, and he slaughtered many thousands of them; and in Ephorus in the first book, the story of the fifty daughters of Thespius, with all of whom, virgins as they were, Heracles is said to have lain at once; and the story of Aristodemus, that he died struck by a thunderbolt. Of factual narratives one may take some from Herodotus, such as the passage in the fourth book about the whole earth being divided into three parts, called Europe, Libya, and Asia; and from Thucydides in the first book, the account of the killing of Hipparchus by Harmodius and Aristogeiton and their party. We may take more from other historians as well: from Ephorus in the first book, the account of the division of the Peloponnese at the return of the Heraclidae; and from Theopompus in the twenty-fifth book of the Philippics, that the so-called Hellenic oath is a fabrication — the oath the Athenians say the Greeks swore before the battle at Plataea against the barbarians — and likewise the treaty of the Athenians with the Greeks concerning King Darius; and further that not all agree that the battle at Marathon happened as it is celebrated, and whatever else, he says, the city of the Athenians boasts of and by which it deceives the Greeks.

Likewise one may find the so-called commonplace among the ancients, such as the Demosthenic passage in the speech On the Crown: for among the Greeks — not among some, but among all alike — there arose so great a crop of traitors and men who took bribes and were hateful to the gods, and what follows. So too Lycurgus against an adulterer in the speech against Lycophron, and Hyperides against courtesans in the speech against Aristagora; and the others we shall set out in the section on commonplaces.

Many things have been described in set descriptions among the ancients too: as in Thucydides, the plague in the second book, and the wall built round Plataea in the third, and elsewhere a sea battle and a cavalry battle; and in Plato, in the Timaeus, the account of Sais; and in Herodotus, in the second book, the seven walls at Ecbatana. We have also, in the ninth book of Theopompus' Philippics, the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, which lies between two great mountains, Ossa and Olympus, with the Peneius flowing through the middle of them, into which all the rivers of Thessaly run together. And in Philistus, in the eighth book, the account of Dionysius the tyrant's preparations against the Carthaginians and the making of the arms and the ships and the engines; and in the eleventh book, the account of his funeral and the elaborate splendour of the pyre.

As for impersonation, what finer example could there be than the poetry of Homer, and the dialogues of Plato and the other Socratics, and the plays of Menander? We have too the encomia of Isocrates, and the funeral orations of Plato and Thucydides and Hyperides and Lysias, and Theopompus' encomium of Philip and of Alexander, and Xenophon's Agesilaus.

There are comparisons among the ancients as well: in Demosthenes, in the speech against Leptines, where he wishes to prefer Conon to Themistocles; and you would find in Xenophon's Symposium Socrates testifying to Callias that the love of the soul is far better than that of the body.

Examples of the exercise of the thesis may be taken from Aristotle and Theophrastus, for many of their books are entitled Theses. Some thesis-headings have already been treated by the orators too; and indeed whole speeches might be reckoned to be virtually theses, such as the speech attributed to Lysias entitled On the Unveiling Gifts, and the one On Abortion. For in the one it is inquired whether a woman being married must keep securely the unveiling gifts that were given her, and in the other whether what is still in the womb is a human being, and whether abortions are matters for which women are not accountable. They say these speeches are not by Lysias; nevertheless it is not without profit for the young to come across these too, for the sake of exercise. It is possible also to find a thesis-heading in every speech, as in Demosthenes' speech against Onetor for ejectment, whether examinations under torture are truthful; and in Aeschines' speech against Timarchus, whether reports are truthful; and other such in other places.

We shall find refutation of laws in abundance in many places among most of the orators, but most completely in Demosthenes, in the speeches against Timocrates and against Aristocrates and against Leptines; and confirmations both in others and in Lysias, in the speech against Diocles concerning the law against the orators. For even if the ancients have not used all the starting points we have handed on — because they composed their speeches not for exercise but for real contests — nevertheless they display the whole disposition of such speeches.

That the ancients did not neglect paraphrase either is clear from what was said a little earlier. Many things have also been worked up more fully by one writer than another: the Cylonian pollution, at any rate, has been elaborated by Thucydides more than by Herodotus and Euphron; and Demosthenes elaborated more than Hyperides the confusion that came upon the Athenians when someone came in the evening to report to the prytaneis that Elatea had been seized. It is possible, too, to set histories and whole speeches side by side and consider which is the better worked out — the speeches of Demosthenes, for instance, against those of Hyperides, and the Hellenic histories of Theopompus against those of Xenophon.

Refutation may best be found in those speeches in which one man accuses and another defends himself on the charges, as in Aeschines' speech against Ctesiphon and Demosthenes' On the Crown, and again in the speech of each On the False Embassy. You would find it in histories too, in Thucydides: in the first book there is the reply of the Corinthians to the Corcyraeans, and in the third that of Diodotus and Cleon. In Plato both elaboration and refutation may be seen at work upon the matters themselves: in the Phaedrus, having spoken on the same subject as Lysias, he then argues against both speeches in turn, his own and that of Lysias; and in the Republic, after at the outset supporting Thrasymachus about justice through the persons of Glaucon and Adeimantus, he immediately afterwards makes his defence against the whole accusation.

I have set these out, not because I think all of them suitable for all beginners, but that we may recognize how thoroughly necessary the practice of the exercises is — not only for those who intend to be orators, but also for anyone who wishes to handle the power of words, whether as a poet or a prose-writer or in any other kind. For these are, as it were, the foundations of every form of discourse; and in whatever way one introduces them into the souls of the young, the same character must necessarily belong to what comes after.

Therefore, besides what has been said, the teacher himself should compose some refutations and confirmations as finely as he can and assign them to the young to recite, so that, being stamped according to that training, they may be able to imitate. And when they have become capable of writing themselves, one must dictate to them the order of the headings and of the arguments, and point out the right moment for digression and for amplification and for all the rest, and make clear also the character of the problem. Attention must be paid too to the composition of the words, teaching them everything by which they will escape composing badly — and above all metrical and rhythmical diction, such as much of the work of Hegesias the orator, and of the so-called Asianic orators, and some of Epicurus, as in what he writes to Idomeneus: O you who from youth have thought all my movements delightful. And of the sayings that circulate as his — though even now we do not find them in his writings — there is: Tell me, Polyaenus, shall we go away together, that great joy may come? Such things are utterly blameworthy and have an obvious badness of composition. But it deserves pardon when a man occasionally falls into those metres which have a likeness to prose, such as the iambic; and therefore all prose writers fall into this kind against their will. Ephorus, at any rate, in his work On Diction, in the very sentence forbidding the use of rhythmical language, has produced a verse at the very beginning, saying: and again about rhythmical diction I shall go through it.

One must hold no less to propriety, so as not to lay bare shameful things outright, but to report them with reserve — as Aeschines, slandering Demosthenes for unspeakable practices, says that he is not clean in his body, not even in the part from which he sends forth his voice. Besides these things, the expression must be both clear and vivid; for one must not merely report, but also make the speech at home in the mind of the hearers, so that what Homer says may come about: I shall speak an easy word and set it in your mind.

Correction is not the removal of all the faults from the outset, but of a few, and especially the obvious ones, so that the young man may not be disheartened and become despondent about what is to come. At the same time, the one correcting should point out on what account the fault arose, and how it is possible to do better. It is much more useful, too, to assign the young to write on some problems already worked out by the ancients — a commonplace, or a narrative, or a description, or an encomium, or a thesis, or something else of the sort — and afterwards to have them come upon the ancients' versions, so that if they have written similarly they may be confirmed, and if not, they may have the ancients themselves as their correctors.

And since we are not all naturally suited to everything — some fall short in the emotions but succeed rather in character-drawing, others the reverse, and others come behind in both but work out their enthymemes better — one must try to increase one's natural advantages and to fill up what is lacking by these increases, so that we may be able to speak well not only on great problems, like Aeschines, nor only on small ones, like Lysias, but may have equipment for both, like Demosthenes. And in all this one must try to learn thoroughly the delivery that is appropriate to each form of speech.
3.1:
A fable is a fictitious account picturing a truth. One must know that our consideration now is not about every fable, but about those to which, after setting them out, we append the account of what it is an image of — though sometimes we state the account first and bring in the fables afterwards.

They are called Aesopic, and Libyan, or Sybaritic, and Phrygian, and Cilician, and Carian, and Egyptian, and Cyprian. There is a single difference among all of these: the particular class attached to each — Aesop said, or a Libyan man, or a Sybarite, or a Cyprian woman, and in the same way with the rest. If there is no addition indicating the class, we call such a fable Aesopic, in the more general sense. Those who say that fables composed about irrational animals are of one sort and those about human beings of another, and the impossible ones of one sort and those keeping to the possible of another, seem to me to be supposing simple-mindedly; for all the forms occur in all the kinds mentioned above.

They are generally called Aesopic, not because Aesop was the first inventor of fables — for Homer and Hesiod and Archilochus and certain others older than he plainly knew them, and indeed Connis the Cilician and Thurus the Sybarite and Cybissus from Libya are mentioned by some as fable-makers — but because Aesop used them more abundantly and more skilfully. It is like the way a metre is called Aristophanic or Sapphic or Alcaic, or is named from one poet or another, not because these poets alone or first invented the metres, but because they used them most.

Of the ancients, the poets call them rather ainoi, and others mythoi; while those who have written in prose most of all favour calling them logoi rather than mythoi, whence they call Aesop a logopoios. Plato, in the dialogue on the soul, names it now a mythos and now a logos. It is called mythos as being a kind of speech, since the ancients used mytheisthai for speaking; and ainos because it also contains some exhortation, for the whole thing is referred to some useful counsel. Nowadays, however, some call riddles ainoi as well.

This exercise proceeds as follows. We recite the fable, and inflect it, and interweave it with a narrative; we expand and compress it; it is also possible to append some account to it, and, when some account has been set forth, to fashion a fable resembling it; and besides these we refute and confirm. What recitation is we have explained in the section on the chreia; but in fables the expression should be simpler and flowing, and, so far as possible, unelaborated and clear. One should therefore learn beforehand as many as can be found so recited among the ancients. It is useful, too, when a whole fable has been given, for the learner to be trained to begin gracefully from within the fable, as Hesiod does when he says that thus the hawk addressed the dapple-necked nightingale; for from what follows — that foolish is he who wishes to contend against the stronger — it is shown that the nightingale was contending with the hawk, and that the hawk, angered, seized her and then spoke thus.

Fables, and the chreia, must be inflected into the numbers and the oblique cases, and one must practise especially with the accusatives, because the ancients recited most of their fables in this way, and quite rightly, as Aristotle says; for they do not speak in their own person, but refer the thing to antiquity, so as to soften the appearance of saying impossible things. But one should not always follow the sequence of the case set at the start as though bound by some law; rather some things should be brought in and a mixed manner used, so that one case is set at the beginning but there is a change in what follows into another — for this variety is the more pleasing. Such is the fable in the Zopyrus of Phaedo the Socratic: it has its beginning from the accusative — they say, Socrates, that the youngest son of the king made someone a present of a lion cub — but a little further on he changed into the nominative thus: and it seems to me that the lion, being reared with the boy, who was by now a young man, followed him wherever he walked, so that the Persians said he was in love with the boy; and so on.

We interweave thus: having set out the fable, we bring in a narrative, as it fits; or conversely the narrative first and the fable afterwards. Take, for example, the invention that a camel, desiring horns, was deprived even of its ears. Having said this first, we shall bring in the narrative in this fashion: Croesus the Lydian seems to me to have suffered something much like this camel — and then the whole narrative about him in order.

We expand by lengthening the impersonations in the fable, and by describing a river or something of the sort; by doing the opposite we compress.

We append an account thus, when, a fable having been told, we undertake to bring in some sententious account resembling it. For example: a dog carrying meat along a river, and seeing his own shadow in the water, supposed it was another dog with a bigger piece of meat; he threw away what he had, and leaping into the river to snatch the other, was drowned. We shall bring in the account thus: that often those who reach for greater things destroy themselves along with what they already have. There may be several appended accounts to a single fable, when we take our starting points from each of the matters in the fable; and conversely a great many fables may be likened to a single account. For when we have set out the force of the appended account in simple terms, we shall assign the young to fashion some fable proper to the matter proposed; and they will be able to do this readily once they have been filled with many fables — some taken up from the ancient writings, some merely heard, and some fashioned by themselves.

We shall refute and confirm in this way. Since the fable-maker himself admits that he writes what is false and impossible, but persuasive and useful, one must refute by showing that what he says is unpersuasive and unprofitable, and confirm from the opposites; for these are the highest headings, under which the particulars fall. The introduction must be suited to the fable; after the introduction one must set out the fable, and sometimes merely cite it — which in a case it is not always necessary to narrate; then one must pass to the argument and refute each of the things said in turn, beginning from the first, trying to be well supplied with arguments for each part of the fable under each topic.

The arguments are to be taken from these topics: from obscurity, from implausibility, from unseemliness, from deficiency, from excess, from the unusual, from self-contradiction, from arrangement, from the unprofitable, from dissimilarity, and from falsehood.

Obscurity arises either through one word or through several: through one, when someone uses words either contrary to usage or ambiguously; through several, when it is possible, with nothing added and nothing taken away, to understand what is said in more ways than one — for example, I made you free, being a slave. For it is not clear whether he made him free instead of a slave, or a slave instead of a free man. We shall speak more precisely about clarity a little later, in the section on narrative.

The implausible is what could have happened or been said, but is disbelieved as to whether it happened or was said: whether because of the person to whom the action or the saying is referred, or because of the place in which something is said to have happened or been said, or because of the time at which it is said to have happened or been said, or because of the manner of the action or the saying, or because of the cause of these same things — when we say that it is not likely that such a man did this or said this, in this place, or at this time, or in this manner, or for this cause. The same account holds for the unseemly as well.

The deficient and the excessive is when he leaves out something that could have been said, or says something that is nothing to the purpose — a person, or an action, or a time, or a manner, or a place, or a cause, or something of the sort.

The unusual is what is said contrary to the accepted story, or contrary to common suppositions: as if someone should say that men were not moulded by Prometheus but by some other of the gods, or should call the ass sensible or the fox witless.

The topic from self-contradiction is when we show the fable-writer contradicting himself; and this is to be used not at the beginning, but when we are refuting something in the middle or at the end, so that we may then show it to be contrary to what was said before.

From arrangement we shall argue by convicting him that what ought to have been said first in the fable was not recited among the first, and what ought to have come at the end was set elsewhere; and generally that each thing, so far as we can manage, was not said in its fitting order.

And indeed the topic from the unprofitable is clear, which we shall use rather for the refutation of the appended account. Those from dissimilarity and from falsehood are refutative of the appended account only: from dissimilarity, when the things in the fable resemble the appended account in nothing, or not in every respect; from falsehood, when it does not turn out in every case as the fable-writer says — that those who reach for more are deprived even of what they have, for this is not always true. From the opposite topics we shall confirm.

One must recapitulate when the refutations and confirmations are many and strong; when they are few and weak, recapitulation is not to be employed. Here too we shall use disparagement, and amplifications or diminutions, and digressions, and characterizations, and in short all the forms of speech; for, as we said, this exercise differs little from a forensic case. The same topics are useful also for the refutation and confirmation of narratives.
4.1:
A narrative is an expository account of things that happened, or are treated as having happened. The elements of narrative are six: the person, whether one or more; the act performed by the person; the place in which the act occurs; the time at which the act occurs; the manner of the act; and sixth, the cause of these things. These being the highest elements, out of which a complete narrative is filled out, a narrative is composed of all of them together with the circumstances attending them; and it is defective if it lacks any one of them.

Attending the person are family, nature, upbringing, disposition, age, fortune, moral choice, action, speech, death, and what comes after death.

Attending the act are great or small, dangerous or free of danger, possible or impossible, easy or difficult, necessary or unnecessary, advantageous or disadvantageous, just or unjust, honourable or dishonourable.

Attending time are the past, the present, and the future; what came first or second and so on; what suits life in our own day and what the ancient world; and above all the appointed terms which men fix, whether in common or privately. Then, whether the thing happened in winter or spring, in summer or autumn; by night or by day; when an assembly was being held, or a procession, or a festival; and whether at a wedding, or the reception of friends, or a time of mourning, or some such circumstance of life.

Attending place are size, distance, a neighbouring city or country; whether the place was sacred or profane, one's own or another's, deserted or inhabited, secure or exposed, level or mountainous, waterless or well watered, bare or wooded, and everything of the same sort.

Attending manner is whether the thing was done unwillingly or willingly; and each of these is divided into three — the unwilling into ignorance, chance, and necessity; the willing into whether it was done by force, or in secret, or by deceit.

Attending the cause of actions is whether it was done for the sake of gaining goods or for release from an evil, or through friendship, or for a woman, or for the sake of children, or through the passions — anger, love, hatred, envy, pity, drunkenness, and the like.
4.2:
The virtues of narrative are three: clarity, conciseness, and plausibility. Best of all, then, if it is possible, the narrative should have all the virtues; but if this is impracticable — since conciseness is in a way opposed both to clarity and to plausibility — one must aim rather at what is pressing. If, for instance, the matter is by nature intricate, one must go for clarity and plausibility; if it is simple and not complicated, for conciseness and plausibility. For one must always hold to the plausible in a narrative, since this belongs to it most properly of all; and when this is not present, the clearer and more concise the narrative is, the more incredible it appears to the hearers.

If the matter is by nature plausible, one should use conciseness in part, but for the most part those things which establish the case and lead the matter proposed toward plausibility. Further, what will distress the hearers must be narrated as concisely as possible — as Homer does: Patroclus lies dead. But on what gives pleasure one should linger, just as the same poet, in dealing with the Phaeacians, who loved stories, made Odysseus narrate his own affairs with great precision and at leisure.
4.3:
A narrative becomes clear from two sources: from the matters reported themselves, and from the diction of the report by which the matters are conveyed.

From the matters themselves: when the things spoken of do not escape common understanding, as those in dialectic and geometry do; and when one does not narrate many things at once, but carries each through to its end. It is on this last point that some bring a charge against Thucydides; for having divided his history by summers and winters, he is often compelled, before the whole matter is finished, to pass over to something else that happened at the same season, and then narrates the remainder of the matter as accomplished in another winter or summer. Sometimes he needed a third and a fourth season before he came to the end of the matter he had begun to narrate, always taking up along with the first narrative the events of each season, so that the matters become at once obscure and hard to remember.

One must guard also against confusing the times and the order of events, and further against saying the same things twice; for this, no less than the rest, confuses the understanding. One must avoid, too, inserting long digressions in the middle of a narrative. For one should not reject every digression outright, as Philistus does — since a digression gives the hearers' understanding a rest — but only one so great in length that it estranges the understanding of the hearers, so that they need to be reminded again of what was said before, as happens in Theopompus in the Philippics. For we find there, I suppose, two and three and more whole histories brought in by way of digression, in which there is not so much as the name of Philip, nor indeed of any Macedonian.

A narrative also becomes obscure through the omission of things that necessarily had to be mentioned, and through allegorizing stories that have been kept hidden.
4.4:
In respect of diction, the man who aims at clarity must guard against using poetic words, coined words, tropical words, archaic words, foreign words, and homonyms.

Poetic words are all those that need some explanation, such as krêgyon, antipherizein, marnasthai, and the like. Coined words are such as kelados, konabos, kelaryzein, and the like. Tropical, for instance: far-seeing Zeus grants a wooden wall to the Trito-born. For by this trope the Pythian god signified to the Athenians that they should leave the city, embark on the ships, and use these as a wall. Archaic words are those customary long ago but now fallen out of use, as Demosthenes says in the speech against Aristocrates, concerning Draco's law, that mêde apoinan means not to exact money; for the ancients called money apoina. Foreign words are those native to some peoples but not customary among the rest — as if someone should call the harbour an agora, as the Thessalians do, or say kleinos instead of 'beloved,' as the Cretans do. Homonyms are words of which the sound and the name are the same, but what is signified by the sound is different — such as pais, for it signifies a son, and a child in respect of age, and a slave.
4.5:
What the dialecticians call ambiguity also makes the expression obscure. It arises from a sequence of letters that reads one way undivided and another way divided — as in the sentence written AULÊTRISPESOUSADÊMOSIAESTÔ. For one thing is the phrase taken as a unit and undivided, let the flute-girl who has fallen be public property; another is the divided form, let the courtyard that has fallen three times be public property.

Ambiguity arises further when it is unclear with what a particle is construed, as in OUKENTAUROISHOHÊRAKLÊSMACHETAI; for it signifies two things — Heracles does not fight with centaurs, and Heracles fights among bulls.

Similarly the phrasing becomes obscure when it is unclear with what a significant word is construed, as in the line: and they, though grieved, laughed sweetly at him. For it is ambiguous whether they were grieved over Thersites, which is false, or over the hauling down of the ships. And again: the people of great-hearted Erechtheus, whom once Athena nurtured, the daughter of Zeus, and the grain-giving earth bore. For it is unclear whether he says that the people or that Erechtheus was nurtured by Athena and borne by the earth. It is through this kind of ambiguity that the books of Heraclitus the philosopher have become dark, since he used it to excess, whether deliberately or through ignorance.

One must observe also not to use transposed word order, such as much of what is found in Thucydides — for we do not reject the class of transpositions altogether, since through it the phrasing becomes varied and not commonplace — nor parentheses, especially long ones; for those that take their resolution close at hand do not trouble the hearers. And indeed leaving out certain words is contrary to clarity.

One must guard, too, against setting cases side by side for different persons, for it becomes ambiguous which one the reference is carried to. In the accusative — the only case in which many think ambiguity arises — there is the example in Demosthenes against Meidias: many know that Euaeon, the brother of Leodamas, killed Boeotus at a dinner. For it is unclear whether Euaeon killed Boeotus or Boeotus Euaeon, which is false; and further, whether the brother of Leodamas is Euaeon or Boeotus. In the nominative, as in Herodotus in the first book: the Egyptians too are Colchians. For it is unclear whether the Egyptians are Colchians or, on the contrary, the Colchians Egyptians. The same holds in the genitive and the dative: the Colchians being Egyptians, and to the Colchians being Egyptians. In the accusative, then, the ambiguity is beyond dispute; but in the other cases it is plain that by the addition of the article the expression is no longer ambiguous — the Colchians are Egyptians — for it has become clear that he is speaking about the Colchians, that they are Egyptians.
4.6:
Similarly the narrative will be concise both from the matters and from the diction. For conciseness is speech that signifies the most essential of the matters, neither adding what is unnecessary nor taking away what is necessary, in respect both of the matters and of the diction.

From the matters: when we neither take many matters together at once, nor insert some into others; and when we leave out whatever seems to be understood along with the rest, and do not begin from far back, nor spend our speech on what is superfluous, as those do who are accustomed to narrate beyond the facts. For these things would perhaps suit history — lengthening, beginning from far back, and working up some matters that seem incidental. But one who is delivering a narrative ought to look to the main point of the whole matter he has proposed, taking into the narrative only what contributes to this. In the case of Cylon, for instance: if someone is writing a history about him, it is fitting to say from what ancestors he came, and who his father and mother were, and a great many other things besides — the contest he contended in at Olympia, and how many victories he carried off, and to name the Olympiads in which he was victorious. But one who is delivering a narrative about him has no business being precise about any of these things, as indeed Herodotus and Thucydides did, each of whom set out to tell of the Cylonian pollution.

In matters of diction one must observe not to use synonyms; for words having the same force make the speech longer with no need, as in Demosthenes in the second Olynthiac: it seems altogether like some divine and heaven-sent benefaction. Nor should one make a phrase in place of a single word — for instance, instead of 'he died,' 'he departed from life,' and all such expressions. Further, whoever wishes to report concisely must strip away along with the rest everything that is understood; and he should use simple words rather than compound ones, and shorter rather than longer, when they signify the same thing. Yet one must take care not to fall unawares, through the desire for conciseness, into vulgarity or obscurity.
4.7:
For the narrative to be plausible, one must adopt expressions proper to the persons and the matters and the places and the occasions, and matters that are likely and consistent with one another. One must also add the causes briefly to the narrative, and state what is disbelieved in a credible way; and in general one should aim at what is fitting to the person and to the other elements of the narrative, both in the matters and in the diction.

Our example will be the narrative at the beginning of the second book of Thucydides about the Plataeans and the Thebans. For it was likely that the Thebans, being always at variance with the Plataeans, on learning that there would be a war, should wish to seize Plataea in advance while it was still peace; and that, having so resolved, they should not make the attempt openly but on a moonless night; and besides this, that they should have some of the Plataeans who would open the gates for them, no guard having been posted because of the treaty; and that those who betrayed the city did so for the sake of a private enmity toward certain of the citizens, whom they meant to destroy when this happened — not that the Thebans had betrayed them.

It is plausible, too, that the Plataeans, perceiving that the city had been suddenly seized by the enemy, supposed because of the night that far more had entered, and so came to terms; but afterwards, realizing that they were not many, attacked them. And the uproar is altogether most plausible: the Plataeans falling upon the Thebans, and at the same time the women and the household slaves from the houses raising a shout and a wailing and pelting the Thebans with stones and tiles; and a heavy rain having come on in the night, many of the Thebans being pursued through mud and darkness and unable to escape through inexperience of the roads.

It is plausible also that someone shut the gates, using the butt-spike of a javelin instead of the pin for the bar; and much more plausible still is the matter of the woman who gave the axe. For it was likely that a woman living near deserted gates, seeing the enemy shut in, should be afraid that, despairing of safety and reduced to desperation, they might turn to doing harm — most of all to whomever they could, but first of all to the neighbouring houses. I say nothing of the fact that it was like a woman to pity even enemies who had been beaten. And so with all the rest, that we may not speak at length.
4.8:
The exercise on the narrative is not of a single form. Just as with the fable, it is recited and inflected and interwoven with a fable, and it is compressed and expanded; further, in the recitation we alter the order of the headings; and besides this it is possible, while keeping the same order, to make the phrasing in many and varied ways. Further still, one may add a comment while narrating, and interweave two or even three narratives with one another in the recitation; and after all these, one may refute and confirm.

Now concerning recitation and inflection and interweaving, and further compression and expansion, we have spoken in the section on fables. The inversion of the order we shall accomplish in many ways. For it is possible to begin from the middle and run back to the beginning, and then to come down to the last events — which is what Homer did in the Odyssey. For he began from the time when Odysseus was with Calypso, then ran back to the beginning with a polished management of his material, since he made Odysseus narrate his own affairs to the Phaeacians; and then, joining on the remaining narrative, he ended with the last events, up to Odysseus' killing of the suitors and his making of friendship with their parents. Thucydides too, beginning from the affairs at Epidamnus, ran back to the fifty years, and then came down to the Peloponnesian War.

It is possible also to begin from the last events and come to the middle, and so to arrive at the beginning — which Herodotus teaches us in his third book, speaking thus: Cambyses, sending a herald to Egypt, asked Amasis for his daughter; and he asked on the advice of an Egyptian man, who did this out of a grudge against Amasis, because Amasis had torn him from his wife and children and handed him over to the Persians. Then he narrates the causes as well: that the king of the Persians had asked from the king of the Egyptians for an eye-doctor, whoever was best. For the natural order of the narrative would have been first to tell of the eye-disease of the king of the Persians, and how, sending to Egypt, he asked from the ruler there for an eye-doctor, and that man sent him up; then that the doctor, taking it hard to be parted from wife and children, avenged himself on the man who had given him up, by advising the king of the Persians to ask for a daughter from the king of the Egyptians, so that either by giving her he should be grieved, or by not giving her should incur enmity.

It is possible, further, to begin from the middle and come to the end, and there to stop; and again to begin from the last events and run back to the beginning and stop at the middle; and further to begin from the first events and pass over to the last, and to cease at the middle.
4.9:
So much, then, for the inversion of the order. Since we are accustomed to bring matters out sometimes as making a statement, sometimes as doing something more than stating; sometimes as asking a question, at other times as inquiring, and sometimes as raising a difficulty; at one time as giving a command, at another as praying; now as swearing an oath, now as addressing someone; at another time as supposing, and sometimes as conversing — it is possible to bring out narratives in all these manners, varying them.

Thucydides, then, at the beginning of the second book of his Histories, brought out this narrative in the manner of one making a statement: Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians.

But if we should wish to do something more than state, we shall say thus: The coming of the Thebans to Plataea proved, it seems, the cause of great events for the Athenians and the Spartans and the allies on either side; for Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia. And so we shall join on the rest of the narrative.

If we should wish to ask a question, we shall say thus: Is it then true that Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia? And in this interrogative fashion we shall go through what follows. We should inquire thus: Who were the Theban men, a little more than three hundred, who entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia? And we shall bring in the rest by way of inquiry.

Raising a difficulty and asking a question differ in no way in the utterance, and therefore we shall be content with one of them; for whether we ask or raise a difficulty, we shall bring it out thus: Is sleeplessness the most talkative of all things? They seem to differ in that the one who asks seeks an answer, while the one who raises a difficulty does not altogether do so, but is merely at a loss within himself.

If we should wish to give a command, we shall do it thus. We shall suppose, in the last part of the narrative, after the destruction of those who entered Plataea, someone exhorting either the Thebans or the Plataeans, in this way: Come, men of Plataea, show yourselves worthy of your city, and of your ancestors who fought against the Persians and Mardonius, and of those who lie buried in your land. Show the Thebans that they act unjustly in thinking you should obey them and be their slaves, and in forcing you by war against your will, contrary to the oaths and the treaties — a little more than three hundred of them, who entered under arms about the time of first sleep into your city, which is an ally of the Athenians. And in the same way we shall narrate what follows as addressed to the Plataeans.

If we should suppose the exhortation to be made to the Thebans, we shall say thus: Come, men of Thebes, show yourselves worthy of yourselves and of your fathers and of the rule you hold over all Boeotia; and show the Plataeans that, being your slaves, they have not only run away to the Athenians but have also destroyed men of yours, a little more than three hundred, who came under arms about the time of first sleep into their Plataea. And in this manner we shall narrate the rest.

It is possible also to make a command in this way, if we should suppose someone commanding the Thebans, before the entry into Plataea took place, to do the very things they did: Come, men of Thebes, let men of yours, a little more than three hundred, enter under arms about the time of first sleep into your own Plataea, which is now an ally of the Athenians. And we shall go through what follows in this manner, so far as it admits of it.

If we should pray, we shall say thus: Would that Theban men, a little more than three hundred, had never entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians. And to the end we shall narrate in the manner of one praying.

It is not obscure in what manner the narrative will be brought out in the form of an oath. The form of address we pass over, because we have already handed it on earlier, among the inflections by cases, under the vocative.

Supposing, we shall say thus: Let us suppose that Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians; and that Naucleides and those with him opened the gates for them, no guard having been posted because of the treaty — and so with what follows.

If we should wish to report in dialogue, we shall suppose certain persons conversing with one another about what was done, the one teaching and the other learning what had happened. For example: Often before now it has occurred to you to ask me about what befell the Thebans and the Plataeans at Plataea; and now too I would gladly hear of it, if you have time to narrate it. — But indeed there is time, and I am telling you at once, if, as you say, you have a desire to hear about these things. The Thebans, being always at variance with the Plataeans, wished to seize Plataea in advance while it was peace. So men of theirs, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into the city, which was an ally of the Athenians. — How then, when it was night and the gates were shut, and moreover a guard was posted, did they easily enter unnoticed? — You have anticipated me a little, since I too was about to say that men opened the gates for them, Naucleides and those with him, no guard having been posted because of the peace — and so on. In the same manner we shall go through it, asking and answering according to the rule of dialectic.

Further, in stating matters we sometimes affirm — for instance, Theon is conversing. But it is possible to bring out narratives not only affirming but also denying: affirming, as we said Thucydides brought out the narrative; denying, for instance — Neither did Theban men, a little more than three hundred, enter under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, which was an ally of the Athenians, nor did Naucleides and those with him open the gates; and so to the end.

There is also another manner, called asyndeton, when we leave out the connectives that bind the phrasing together — for instance: Theban men, a little more than three hundred, entered under arms about the time of first sleep into Plataea in Boeotia, an ally of the Athenians; Naucleides and those with him opened the gates for them; they placed their arms in the market-place. And similarly with what follows. So too in Demosthenes: Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea, Halonnesus — I mention none of these. And again: But he is gone to the Hellespont; earlier he came against Ambracia; he holds Elis, so great a city in the Peloponnese; he plotted against Megara the other day.

It is possible also to interweave these manners with one another and to make a mixture of two or more, so as to report some parts of the narrative in the manner of one making a statement, others without connectives, and others in whatever way one wishes, varying the phrasing.
4.10:
To add a comment to a narrative is to append a maxim to each part of the narrative. Such a thing suits neither history nor a political speech, but is rather adapted to the theatre and the stage. Therefore it occurs most abundantly among poets of that kind, as in Menander in many places, and at the beginning of both the Dardanus and the Recruiter: the son of a poor man, brought up with no resources, was ashamed to see his father possessing little; for having been well educated, he straightway rendered a fine fruit. For the last line is added superfluously, merely hunting the applause of the spectators.

When, however, one mixes such maxims in continuously and they pass unnoticed, the narrative becomes in a way charming — as in Herodotus in the first book. For speaking about human life, that it is not stable but has many changes in itself, and then reckoning up of how many days a human life consists, namely seventy years, he adds: of all these days not one brings on anything at all like another. Then he adds the comment in this manner: thus, Croesus, man is wholly chance. So too Gyges says to Candaules: master, what unsound proposal is this, bidding me look upon my mistress naked? For a woman puts off her modesty along with her tunic.

And indeed we might find the same among the orators, not least in the most political of writers, Demosthenes, and in his most political speeches. For in the second Olynthiac, narrating about Philip that he keeps about him mimes of ridiculous things and composers of shameful songs — men whom the city of the Athenians expelled as being utterly licentious — and that Philip, being such a man, naturally escapes the notice of everyone through his success in war, he afterwards adds the comment: for successes are terribly apt to conceal and overshadow such disgraces.

It is possible also, conversely, to set a sententious statement first and then narrate, just as we noted in the case of the fable — as in Menander, in The Worthy Heiress: is sleeplessness the most talkative of all things? and then the narrative follows: it has roused me and brought me out here to tell my whole life from the beginning.
4.11: To interweave one narrative with another is when we undertake to narrate two or even more narratives at once. The school of Isocrates practised this especially, and Isocrates himself in the Panegyricus, thus: there came the children of Heracles, and a little before them Adrastus the son of Talaus, king of Argos, the latter having met with misfortune from the expedition against Thebes — and so on. And again: for while Greece was still lowly, there came into our land the Thracians with Eumolpus the son of Poseidon, and the Scythians with the Amazons, the daughters of Ares, not at the same time — and so on.
4.12:
Concerning refutation and confirmation we have said that the same topics are useful as for the fables; but in narratives the topics from falsehood and from impossibility are fitting as well. This is what Thucydides does in refuting the view that Hipparchus was killed by Harmodius and Aristogeiton and their party while he was tyrant; and Herodotus, in opposing those who declare that Cambyses was Egyptian on his mother's side.

It is not always possible to argue from all the topics in narratives; but whenever it can be done, we shall use this order. First from obscurity, in all the ways we spoke of concerning clarity. Second we shall argue from impossibility, showing that it was impossible for the matter to have happened as the writer says — either because it is not in the nature of things to happen at all, or because the events recorded do not fall in the same period of time. So, for instance, against those who say that Heracles killed Busiris; for according to Hesiod, Busiris is older than Heracles by eleven generations. And in general, for many such cases we shall have starting points for our arguments from the refutations of Arion.

Next, even if we grant that the matter is possible, it must be said that it is implausible; and if it is plausible, we shall consider whether it is false; and if it appears true, we shall next inquire whether something is deficient or excessive; and then that the writer contradicts himself in the course of the narrative. Besides these, we shall find fault with the order of the headings, if it has not been arranged fittingly. And if all these things have been suitably disposed, it must nevertheless be shown to be unseemly and unprofitable. For there are matters which ought not to have been done, and which, once done, it is better to pass over in silence — as if someone, having said that Locrian Ajax committed such impieties against Athena as are reported, should then suppose that he suffered no harm either at sea or at home, but died in old age in prosperity.

We shall readily be well supplied with more arguments if, in arguing from each of the topics handed on, we use also the so-called elements out of which every action is constituted: these are the ones we mentioned before — person, act, place, time, manner, and cause.
4.13:
For the sake of example, let our discussion be on a single topic, that of implausibility. If, then, we are refuting the narrative from implausibility, we shall proceed thus, showing that the person is implausible, and the act, and the place in which the act occurred, and likewise the time and the manner and the cause of the act.

Take the case of Medea. From the person: that it is implausible for a mother to do harm to her children. From the act: that it is not likely she cut their throats. From the place: that she would not have killed them in Corinth, where Jason, the children's father, was staying. From the time: that it is implausible at that particular time, when she herself had been humbled, cast out by her husband, a foreign woman, while Jason had acquired greater power by marrying Glauce, the daughter of Creon the king of those parts. From the manner: that she would have tried to escape notice, and would not have made away with them by the sword but by a drug — especially as she was a sorceress. From the cause: that it is implausible that she killed the children through anger against her husband; for the misfortune was not Jason's alone but common to her as well, and hers the more, inasmuch as women are somehow softer in the face of suffering.

In the same way we shall go over the other topics too, arguing according to the successive elements from whichever we can; and from the opposite topics we shall confirm.

These same topics are fitting also for mythical narratives, both those told by the poets and those told by the historians about gods and heroes, and further about creatures altered from their nature, such as some record concerning Pegasus and Erichthonius and the Chimaera and the Hippocentaurs and the like.

But not merely to refute such tales, but also to show the source from which such an account has slipped in, belongs to a more complete competence than most men possess. This is what Herodotus did in the second book, narrating about the doves — how they flew out of Egypt, and one came to Dodona and the other to the shrine of Ammon. Explaining the tale, he says that certain maidens from Egyptian Thebes were priestesses, one of whom was sold to Dodona and the other to the shrine of Ammon; and since they spoke in a foreign tongue and unintelligibly to the natives, an account prevailed that they were birds. Plato too, in the Phaedrus, not accepting the narrative about Oreithyia and Boreas, says that a blast of the north wind pushed Oreithyia down the rocks nearby while she was playing with Pharmaceia, and that thus it came to be said that she had been snatched away by Boreas.

And indeed Ephorus in the fourth book uses this manner: that Tityus was a ruler of Panopeus, a lawless and violent man; that Python was bestial in nature and nicknamed the Serpent; and that those who inhabited the place formerly called Phlegra and now named Pallene were savage men, temple-robbers and eaters of human flesh, the so-called Giants, whom Heracles is said to have subdued after taking Troy; and that, because Heracles and his men, being few, prevailed over the Giants, who were many and impious, the affair of the battle seemed to everyone to have been the work of gods. He resolves many other such tales as well, about Lycurgus and Minos and Rhadamanthus and Zeus and the Curetes and the other things told as myths in Crete.

Palaephatus the Peripatetic also has a whole book entitled On Incredible Things, in which he resolves such matters: for instance, that those first seen riding on horses were supposed to be Centaurs; that Diomedes the Thracian, having exhausted his substance on horse-breeding, was said to have been destroyed by his own horses; and by the same account Actaeon by his dogs; and that Medea, by dyeing the grey hairs on people's heads and making them black, got the reputation of cutting old men up into a cauldron and making them young; and things like these.
4.14: So much, then, for the manners of the exercise; and note that it is possible to train by these same manners in the fables as well.
5.1: A chreia is a concise statement or action, aptly attributed to a definite person or to something corresponding to a person. Closely related to it are the maxim and the reminiscence: for every concise maxim attributed to a person makes a chreia, and the reminiscence too is an action or a saying useful for life. The maxim differs from the chreia in these four respects: that the chreia is always attributed to a person, the maxim not always; that the chreia sometimes states a general truth and sometimes a particular one, whereas the maxim states only the general; further, that the chreia sometimes makes a joke and has nothing useful for life in it, whereas the maxim always concerns what is useful in life; and fourth, that the chreia is an action or a saying, while the maxim is a saying only. The reminiscence is marked off from the chreia in these two respects: the chreia is concise, whereas the reminiscence is sometimes extended; and the chreia is attributed to particular persons, whereas the reminiscence is remembered also for its own sake. It is called chreia par excellence because, more than the others, it is useful for many purposes in life — just as, though there are many poets, we are accustomed to call Homer alone “the Poet” par excellence.
5.2: Of the chreia there are three highest classes: some are verbal, some active, and some mixed. Verbal are those that have their force through words, without an action — for example, Diogenes the philosopher, when someone asked him how he might become famous, answered, “By caring as little as possible about fame.” Of the verbal there are two species, the declarative and the responsive. Of the declarative, some are by voluntary statement — for example, Isocrates the sophist used to say that gifted students are children of gods; others arise out of a circumstance — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a rich but uneducated youth, said, “This fellow is filth plated with silver”; for Diogenes did not simply make the statement, but out of what he saw. Again, of the responsive there are four species: that by [yes-or-no] question, that by inquiry, that by question with a reason attached, and the one called responsive by the same name as its class. A question differs from an inquiry in that to a question one need only assent or deny — nod or shake the head, or answer with a yes or a no — whereas an inquiry demands a longer answer. An example by question: Pittacus of Mytilene, asked whether a man doing something wicked escapes the notice of the gods, said, “No — not even in intending it”; for what is added after the denial is superfluous, since the denial would have sufficed even if it were taken away. The inquiry type is like this: Theano the Pythagorean philosopher, asked by someone how soon after being with a man a woman may go down to the Thesmophorion pure, said, “After her own husband, at once; after another’s, never.” Those by question with a reason are such as contain, besides the answer to the question, some cause or advice or the like — for example, Socrates, asked whether the king of the Persians seemed to him happy, said, “I cannot say, since I do not even know how he stands in education.” Responsive [in the narrow sense] are those that come neither by question nor by inquiry, but where there is some remark to which the reply is made — for example, once when Diogenes was lunching in the marketplace and called him over to lunch, Plato said, “Diogenes, how charming your lack of affectation would be, if it were not affected”; for Diogenes was not asking Plato about anything, nor is Plato inquiring of him, but simply invites him to lunch, which belongs to neither kind. Besides these there is another species falling among the verbal chreiai, called double. A double chreia is one containing the statements of two persons, either of which by itself, with one person, makes a chreia — for example, Alexander king of the Macedonians, standing over Diogenes as he slept, said, “A man who is a counsellor should not sleep the whole night through,” and Diogenes replied, “— one to whom the peoples are entrusted and who has so many cares”; for it would have been a chreia even so, without the reply added. Active are those that reveal some thought without speech. Of the active, some are agentive and some passive. Agentive are those that show some action — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a greedy boy, struck his tutor with his staff. Passive are those that signify something suffered — for example, Didymus the flute-player, convicted of adultery, was hanged by the part his name denotes. Mixed are those that share in both the verbal and the active but have their force in the active — for example, Pythagoras the philosopher, asked how long the life of men is, went up to his bedroom and looked out for a moment, showing by this its brevity. And again, when someone asked a Laconian where the Lacedaemonians have the boundaries of their land, he pointed to his spear.
5.3: These, then, are the species of chreiai. They are delivered: some as maxims, some with proof, some as a witticism, some by syllogism, some by enthymeme, some by example, some as a wish, some symbolically, some figuratively, some by ambiguity, some by a shift of subject, and some in combination, composed of whichever of the aforesaid modes. As a maxim: Bion the sophist used to say that the love of money is the mother-city of all vice. With proof: Isocrates the orator used to urge his pupils to honour their teachers above their parents, because parents are the cause of living only, but teachers of living well — for Isocrates brought out his statement together with its proof. As a witticism: Olympias, learning that her son Alexander was declaring himself the son of Zeus, said, “Will this fellow never stop slandering me to Hera?” By syllogism: Diogenes the philosopher, seeing a youth excessively adorned, said, “If it is for men, you are unlucky; if for women, you do wrong.” By enthymeme: when a companion, Apollodorus, said to Socrates the philosopher, “The Athenians have condemned you to death unjustly,” he laughed and said, “And would you have preferred justly?” — for we must supply the further thought that it is better to be condemned unjustly than justly, which seems to be left out of the chreia though it is conveyed by implication. By example: Alexander king of the Macedonians, urged by his friends to amass money, said, “But these things did not profit Croesus either.” As a wish: Damon the trainer, who was lame in the feet, when his shoes were stolen said, “May they fit the thief.” Symbolically: Alexander king of the Macedonians, asked by someone where he kept his treasures, said, “In these,” pointing to his friends. Figuratively: Plato the philosopher said that the shoots of virtue grow by sweat and toil. By ambiguity: when a boy was being introduced to Isocrates the orator and the one introducing him asked what the boy needed, he said, “A ΚΑΙΝΟΥ writing-tablet and a ΚΑΙΝΟΥ stylus” — for it is ambiguous whether he means a tablet and a mind (καὶ νοῦ), or a new (καινοῦ) tablet and a new stylus. It is by a shift of subject when the one answering transfers what is said and asked to something else — for example, when some men over their drinks were inquiring which was the better flute-player, Antigenidas or Satyrus, Pyrrhus king of the Epirotes said, “For my part, Polysperchon — as a general.” The combined mode plainly comes about in many ways: a witticism may be interwoven with a maxim, or an example with a symbol, or ambiguity with a shift of subject, or generally in as many other ways as a pairing can be made, with two or even more modes taken up into a single chreia — for example, Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, seeing a youth born of an adulterer throwing stones in the marketplace, said, “Stop, boy, or you may hit your father without knowing it”; for the saying is at once symbolic and witty.
5.4: Students are exercised on chreiai by recitation, by inflection, by comment, and by objection; we also expand and compress the chreia, and besides these we refute and confirm it. Recitation is straightforward: when a chreia has been stated, we try to render it as clearly as we can, either in the very same words or in others. Inflection is various: we vary the persons in the chreia through the three numbers, and this not simply, but as one to one, two to two, and several to several; and again two to one, to two, and to several; and further several to one, to two, and to several. For when the chreia has been set out — that Isocrates the orator used to say the gifted are children of gods — we inflect it thus: one to one, “Isocrates the orator used to say that the gifted student is a child of gods”; two to two [in the dual], “The two Isocrateses, the two orators, used to say that the two gifted students are children of gods”; several to several, “The Isocrateses, the orators, used to say that the gifted students are children of gods.” It is clear from these how we shall inflect the other ways as well, for they are transferred into the five cases too. But since some chreiai are verbal, some active, and some mixed from both, and these again have further species, we shall try to teach the inflection of each of them by an example. The nominative presents no difficulty, for each of the chreiai is normally delivered in it. The genitive we shall inflect thus: if the chreia is verbal, we shall add to it “the saying was remembered,” or “a saying is recorded of him when he said.” The former is fitting to append after the whole chreia has been recited — for example, “Isocrates the orator saying that gifted students are children of gods, the saying was remembered”; the second is used in the middle of it, as the statement begins — for example, “Pittacus of Mytilene being asked whether a man doing something wicked escapes the notice of the gods, a saying is recorded of him when he said: not even in intending it.” “A saying is recorded” suits all the verbal chreiai better, except the one by voluntary statement; for that one takes “the saying was remembered.” If the chreia is active: should it be passive, one must add “what befell him was remembered”; should it be agentive, “what was done was remembered”; and similarly with the mixed. Each of these is to be added at the end of the chreia — for example, “Didymus the flute-player being convicted of adultery and hanged by the part his name denotes, what befell him was remembered”; and “Diogenes the Cynic philosopher seeing a greedy boy and striking his tutor with his staff, what was done was remembered.” To the dative, in every chreia except the passive, we shall add “it seemed good,” or “it appeared,” or “it occurred,” or “it came to him,” or something of the sort — for example, “To Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth, it seemed good to say: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” In the passive we shall add “it happened” — for example, “To Didymus the flute-player, convicted of adultery, it happened that he was hanged by the part his name denotes.” To the accusative we shall add, generally in every chreia, “they say” or “it is said” — for example, “Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth, they say (or, it is said) said: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” The vocative is clear: we shall address our words to the person as though he were present, to whom the chreia is attributed — for example, “Diogenes, Cynic philosopher, on seeing a rich uneducated youth you said: This fellow is filth plated with silver.” To comment is to approve what has been said in the chreia, aptly and concisely: either that it is true, or that it is noble, or that it is advantageous, or that other men of proven worth held this same view. For example, Euripides the poet said that the mind of each of us is a god. We shall comment from truth thus: “for the mind is indeed a god to each man, urging us on to what is advantageous and holding us back from what does harm.” From the noble thus: “for it is a noble thing that each man should think the god to be not in gold and silver but in himself.” From the advantageous thus: “so that we may not, supposing that what punishes lies far off, have great readiness to do wrong.” From the testimony of the renowned, when we say that a sage, or a lawgiver, or a poet, or some other famous man is of one mind with what was said: for the chreia before us we shall say, “Such is the mind of men upon the earth as the father of men and gods brings on the day.” We object to chreiai from the contraries — as against Isocrates, when he said that teachers are to be honoured above fathers, since fathers furnished us living but teachers living well: for in objecting we say that there could be no living well, had not fathers first furnished the living. One must know that it is not possible to object to every chreia, since many are expressed well and blamelessly — just as it is not possible to praise them all, since with some the absurdity strikes one at once. We expand the chreia whenever we lengthen the questions and answers in it, and any action or experience contained in it; we compress by doing the opposite. A concise chreia, for example: “Epaminondas, dying childless, said to his friends…” — and we need more besides for it. (†) [Refutation may be drawn] from impossibility, as we might say against Isocrates that it is not possible for men to be born of gods, not even if they are gifted; from implausibility, that it is not likely that Antisthenes, an Athenian, having come from Athens to Lacedaemon, should say that he was passing from the women’s quarters into the men’s; from falsehood, that Bion did not speak truly in saying that the love of money is the mother-city of vice, for folly is more so; from the disadvantageous, that Simonides gives harmful advice in urging us to play in life and to be serious about nothing at all; from uselessness, as when what was said should appear of no benefit at all for life; from shamefulness, whenever we show the chreia to be shameful and open to reproach — for example, a man of Sybaris, seeing the Lacedaemonians living laboriously, said he did not wonder that in their wars they do not shrink from dying, since death is better than such a life; for he made his statement in a thoroughly soft manner, and not after a manly fashion. From these topics, then, one must refute; and one must argue against each part of the chreia, beginning from the first, from as many topics as prove possible — for let it not escape us that it is not possible in every chreia to argue from them all.
5.5: We shall arrange the arguments in the same order in which we set out the topics; and the same topics would serve also for the refutation and the confirmation of maxims. Those who are already more advanced should take their starting points from what we shall set out for the theses as well. The introduction must not be of such a kind as to fit other chreiai, but proper to the one at hand; and this will be done well, in the case of the chreia and the fable and all the rest, when we take the starting points of our introductions from one or two of the highest divisions. After the introduction one must set out the chreia itself, and then the arguments in order. Here one should use amplifications and digressions and characterizations, wherever they are possible.
